evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[3]
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形): a hanging percussion instrument (bell), originally identical to the left side of 㱿. Later phonetically borrowed to represent 南 (OC *nuːm, “south”).
Sagart (1988) instead proposes that it is a pictogram (象形) of the front of a house. Archaeological evidence confirms that in antiquity, at least in some regions, houses were built to face south.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *g-nam (“sky, sun”) (STEDT; Schuessler (2007); Benedict (1972)); the south is traditionally associated with the sun & light, compare 陽 (OC *laŋ, “light, sun-lit south-side of a hill”).
: If so, cognate with Tibetan གནམ (gnam, “sky”), ནམ (nam, “night”), Tshangla ngam (“sun, noon, day, sky”), Chepang न्याम् (nyam, “sun, sunlight, storm-cloud, weather”).
Alternatively, Sagart (2004) relates this word to Old Chinese *nɨm (revised to *nˤ[ə]m in 2014) "belly, front of the body", further "south" to Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-nam (“rib(s)”), as one term for one body-part often shifts its meaning to another body-part nearby.
: If so, 南 is cognate with 妊 (OC *njɯms, “to carry inside one's belly → to be pregnant”), 任 (OC *njɯm, *njɯms, “to carry a burden, especially in front of the body”), also 腩 (OC *nuːmʔ, “belly (of an ox)”), Southern Pumi nõ⁵⁵, Burmese နံရိုး (nam-rui:, “side of the body, rib”), and thus is a semantic counterpart to 北 (OC *pɯːɡ, “north”), which is related to 背 (OC *pɯːɡs, *bɯːɡs, “back of the body”).

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 online text, based on the received text and Duan Yucai's commentary
evidence.field: entry 南; graphic analysis and historical gloss
evidence.text: The entry gives 南 as “艸木至南方，有枝任也。从𣎵𢆉聲” and separately labels 𡴖 “古文.” Duan Yucai interprets the gloss through flourishing summer vegetation and says 𢆉 is phonetic. This is the received Han-era account, not direct confirmation of the graph’s original pictorial source.
evidence.title: 說文解字「南」

evidence.source: Huang Bo, article hosted by Fudan University Center for Research and Preservation of Excavated Texts (via LingLab)
evidence.field: abstract; discussion of oracle-bone forms and uses
evidence.text: Huang proposes that the oracle-bone graph was the original graph for 醓, depicting a lidded cylindrical vessel with a plant-like form above, and that its original sense was meat sauce. He reports oracle-bone uses for direction, the ancestor name 南庚, and a sacrificial item. The article reviews older bell/instrument and animal-young interpretations, and notes disagreement over the sacrificial-item reading; its new 醓 proposal is an argued analysis, not settled consensus.
evidence.title: 《出土文献》 | 黄博：甲骨文“南”及相关字补说（上）

evidence.source: Huang Bo, article hosted by Fudan University Center for Research and Preservation of Excavated Texts (via LingLab)
evidence.field: sections II–III; cited oracle-bone examples and prior interpretations
evidence.text: The article identifies direction, 南 in the ancestor name 南庚, and a sacrificial-item use in oracle-bone inscriptions. It discusses Guo Moruo’s bell-like instrument account and subsequent objections, including problems matching the graph and sacrificial contexts; it also describes proposed readings of the offering as 腩 or 醓 and says the earlier study it reviews left that question open. These Shang inscription examples attest different uses of the written graph, but the article does not establish the semantic chronology among them or prove that the directional word originated as a loan from an instrument name.
evidence.title: 《出土文献》 | 黄博：甲骨文“南”及相关字补说（上）

evidence.source: Laurent Sagart, “The Chinese names of the four directions”
evidence.field: sections on 南 and the direction terms
evidence.text: Sagart reports the four direction characters as attested in Shang epigraphy, giving Middle Chinese 南 nom. He proposes a lexical relation between ‘south’ and an Old Chinese root *nim ‘belly/front of body,’ with 妊 and 任 as related words, and compares 南’s graphic form to a house front. This is a word-etymology proposal distinct from proof of the graph’s formation; the source presents it as an analysis, not a demonstrated consensus.
evidence.title: The Chinese names of the four directions

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The oracle-bone graph’s depicted object remains disputed: bell or percussion instrument, house front, helmet, and Huang Bo’s lidded-vessel analysis have appeared in scholarship. The consulted evidence does not settle the original referent.

The article reports directional, ancestral-name, and sacrificial-item uses in Shang oracle-bone records, but the semantic chronology among these uses is not established here. In particular, a proposed whole-graph sound loan from an instrument cannot be confirmed: the instrument’s identity and ancient name/pronunciation are not independently established.

The early sacrificial use is contested. Huang Bo proposes 醓/meat sauce; prior analyses include 腩 and instrument interpretations. It is unsafe to equate this use with the character’s origin or treat the proposal as consensus.

The proposed ‘front of body/belly’ etymology for the spoken word ‘south’ is a lexical hypothesis, not established graphic derivation. Its proposed source words are not independently shown here to prove a secure semantic chain.

The Shuowen analysis identifies 𣎵 as a semantic element and 𢆉 as phonetic, but the accessed evidence does not independently establish the pronunciations needed to verify the proposed sound relation of 𢆉 to 南. No component role should be asserted from the Shuowen report alone as settled paleographic fact.

The official Unicode GetUnihanData record URL was attempted but inaccessible. Current nán is supported by local Unihan rows only, not by an inspected official upstream page. No additional component reading was needed for the formation hypotheses checked.

No reliable date for a first individual 南 inscription was established beyond the source’s broad report of Shang epigraphic attestation; specific specimen dates and graphic-stage continuity remain unverified.
No bulk extract is recommended: the inspected sources provide character-specific claims, but no verified reuse grant for creating a repeatable local extract was established.

The exact earliest inscription for 南 and the dates of particular inscriptions were not established. Oracle-bone attestation is broad; the discussed article supplies catalogue references but not a securely dated first instance.

The reported Shang uses include direction, the ancestor name 南庚, and a sacrificial item; their semantic chronology is not established. No transition from an object-name to the directional word is demonstrated.

The original depicted referent remains disputed among instrument, house/front, helmet, and Huang Bo's vessel proposal. No independently recoverable ancient name and pronunciation for a putative instrument was found, so a whole-graph loan from that name is unverified.
The proposed relationship between spoken 'south' and a belly/front-of-body word is lexical speculation and does not establish graphic origin. A semantic path remains unproven.

Shuowen's received analysis 从𣎵𢆉聲 is present in the dossier, but this fresh pass did not independently inspect a readable primary Shuowen entry or verify 𢆉 and 南 pronunciations within one reconstruction system. Do not present that component analysis as independently demonstrated here.

The current Unihan kMandarin value could not be verified on the exact official Unicode character page. The local row supports nán locally only; Unicode lookup documentation is not character-specific evidence.

Academia Sinica Xiaoxuetang's exact query and rights pages did not expose readable text to the browser, so no direct Xiaoxuetang candidate or image was selected. A Commons digital redraw with a verified exact file page and CC0 terms was available instead.
No tracked bulk extract is recommended: no explicit reuse grant for bulk character or dictionary text was verified, and the specific claims can be cited at character-level pages.

The acquisition findings mark the Commons 南-oracle.svg candidate unavailable after a 404. Although its description page and exact original-image link were externally inspected, this candidate cannot be returned; the original link also produced a cache-miss error when opened. The Xiaoxuetang query candidate set is unavailable after HTTP 401. No alternate image with both verified identity/provenance and usable acquisition was established in this pass, so no image is proposed.

The original referent of the Shang graph remains disputed: bell/percussion instrument, vessel associated with Huang Bo's 醓 proposal, and other interpretations appear in the reviewed material. A specific archaeological specimen date and a securely dated first instance were not established.

Reported Shang uses include the direction, an ancestor name, and a sacrificial item; their semantic chronology is not established. No independent ancient name and pronunciation for a putative instrument were established, so the proposed whole-graph sound loan from an instrument name remains unverified.

Shuowen's 𣎵 semantic / 𢆉 phonetic analysis is a received historical account. This pass found no adequate reconstruction-system-matched comparison of 𢆉 and 南 to independently confirm the phonetic relationship. No phonetic role is asserted as demonstrated.
No source in this pass establishes a semantic path from a belly/front-of-body word to 'south'; this lexical proposal does not establish graphic formation.

limitations.text: No verifiable glyph image is available to illustrate 南’s early form or its graphic history. The proposed oracle-style redraw has no usable image link, and no alternate image was established with both verified identity and accessible image data.
